Chapter 1

Project Title & Executive Overview

The official title of this engineering and data science capstone project is:

Leftover Radar: AI-Powered Campus Cafeteria Demand Forecasting, Newsvendor Prep Buffer Optimization & Food Waste Mitigation Platform

Leftover Radar is an enterprise-grade, full-stack decision-support instrument engineered specifically for university cafeterias, corporate dining halls, and multi-service institutional catering operations. Institutional kitchens operate under rigorous financial and temporal constraints. Every morning before dawn, head chefs and food service managers must make irrevocable production decisions: exactly how many portions of 20 to 30 distinct menu items must be prepped for breakfast, lunch, and dinner services.

Traditional commercial kitchens rely on crude heuristics, fixed-batch historical rules of thumb, or intuitive guesswork. These naive methods routinely lead to massive operational failures: over-preparing perishable dishes generates severe organic food waste ($₹30 - ₹50$ per dish in direct ingredient loss, landfill emissions, and wasted labor), while under-preparing causes rapid stockouts, diner dissatisfaction, and chaotic mid-service emergency cooking.

Unlike consumer-facing apps that make ungrounded claims about "predicting food waste", Leftover Radar solves the underlying operational root cause through five foundational engineering pillars:

  1. Demand Forecasting, Not Waste Guessing: Directly models consumer appetite ($y = ext{portions\_sold}$) across temporal lags, weather shocks, day-of-week seasonality, academic exam calendars, and cross-item menu cannibalization.
  2. Censored Demand Awareness: Identifies service events where dishes sold out before service closure ($ ext{portions\_sold} == ext{portions\_prepared}$). Unconstrained consumer demand was artificially truncated by kitchen capacity; treating censored points as true demand biases future models downward. Leftover Radar isolates censored points during calibration.
  3. Distribution-Free Split-Conformal Prediction: Rather than providing fragile point estimates, the system computes non-parametric non-conformity intervals providing exact finite-sample coverage guarantees ($98.05\%$ empirical coverage on unseen future dates against a $95\%$ target).
  4. Newsvendor Economic Optimization: Balances asymmetric commercial loss ($c_s$ stockout penalty vs $c_w$ spoilage cost) via the classical operations research critical fractile ($q^* = c_s / (c_s + c_w)$) to generate mathematically optimal prep buffers.
  5. NoSQL High-Velocity Data Architecture: Leverages MongoDB 8.x with WiredTiger document persistence, `$jsonSchema` schema enforcement, compound spatial/temporal indexes, and four production aggregation pipelines executing analytical telemetry in sub-35 milliseconds.
Chapter 2

Problem Statement

Institutional food service operations operate under high stochastic volatility and severe loss asymmetry. In an educational or corporate campus environment, dining demand varies widely day-to-day due to non-linear exogenous drivers that cannot be captured by simple averages.

2.1 The Asymmetric Kitchen Loss Dilemma

In food preparation, the cost of under-preparation ($c_s$, stockout cost) is economically and operationally fundamentally distinct from the cost of over-preparation ($c_w$, waste cost):

  • Over-Preparation Penalty ($c_w$): Prepped portions that remain unsold at the end of a meal period cannot be legally or safely re-served. They represent direct write-offs of raw material ingredients, energy, and labor, contributing to municipal solid waste and methane generation.
  • Under-Preparation Penalty ($c_s$): Running out of a core staple (e.g., Dal Tadka or Rice Bowl) 45 minutes before service ends causes immediate diner dissatisfaction, contract SLA penalties, queue gridlock, and high-stress emergency batch cooking using expensive expedited ingredients.
ext{Total Daily Expected Loss} = \mathbb{E}\left[ c_w \cdot \max(Q - Y, 0) + c_s \cdot \max(Y - Q, 0) ight]

Where $Q$ represents the scheduled kitchen preparation target and $Y$ represents true stochastic consumer demand. Naive regression models minimizing Mean Squared Error (MSE) assume symmetric Gaussian losses ($c_w = c_s$), which produces prep targets that systematically under-prepare high-margin items or over-prepare volatile specialty dishes.

2.2 Exogenous Campus Shocks & Menu Cannibalization

Institutional dining halls do not behave like commercial a-la-carte restaurants. Attendance and item selection are dictated by tightly coupled campus-specific variables:

  • Academic Calendar Cycles: During mid-term and final examination weeks, dining hall footfall spikes by 35% during late-night dinner services, while breakfast attendance drops as students skip morning lectures. Cultural festivals and sports meets draw external visitors, shifting dietary demand toward fast-casual snacks.
  • Meteorological Shocks: Sudden heavy precipitation ($>15 ext{ mm}$) prevents students from leaving campus to visit local external eateries, trapping 100% of the campus population inside the dining hall and increasing meal demand by up to 40%. Extreme ambient heat suppresses hot soup and heavy curry consumption in favor of cold beverages.
  • Menu Cannibalization: Menu items compete directly for a finite student stomach share. When a premium high-velocity item (e.g., Chicken Biryani or Paneer Rice Bowl) is introduced to the lunch cycle, demand for adjacent staples (e.g., Dal Tadka or Egg Curry) drops by 30% to 45%. Static univariate forecasting models fail to model cross-item cannibalization.

2.3 The Censored Point-of-Sale Observation Problem

Standard point-of-sale (POS) registers record only completed sales transactions. If a cafeteria prepares 80 servings of Masala Dosa and all 80 sell out by 9:15 AM (with breakfast concluding at 10:30 AM), recorded sales equal 80. True consumer demand may have been 125 portions. Feeding recorded sales as ground truth into supervised machine learning introduces severe downward target bias, training the model to perpetuate shortages. A robust system must classify and handle right-censored observation records.

Chapter 3

Objective of the Project

The primary objective of this project is to architect, implement, calibrate, and validate a production-ready, full-stack decision-support platform that transforms cafeteria demand forecasting from heuristic guesswork into an empirical, data-driven science.

3.1 Specific Technical & Operational Objectives

  1. Enterprise NoSQL Database Engineering: Design and deploy a MongoDB 8.x document database utilizing PyMongo, featuring strict `$jsonSchema` collection validators, compound multi-key indexes (`(service_date, service_period, item_id)`), and native WiredTiger compression for six core operational collections.
  2. Native Analytical Aggregation Pipelines: Implement four server-side MongoDB aggregation pipelines (`$match`, `$lookup`, `$facet`, `$setWindowFields`, `$dateTrunc`) to execute telemetry analytics, moving-average waste calculations, and forecast-vs-actual joins with sub-35ms query latency.
  3. Zero-Data-Leakage Feature Extraction: Build a 26-feature vectorized engineering pipeline capturing temporal velocity (7-day and 14-day lags, rolling medians, day-of-week seasonality), academic calendar phases, meteorological features, and cross-item competitor presence strictly using pre-service information.
  4. Log1p Inductive Bias Modeling: Develop a supervised regression model utilizing target transformation ($\log(y + 1)$) to inherently enforce strictly non-negative demand predictions and model percentage-based multiplicative feature effects.
  5. Walk-Forward Cross-Validation: Implement an expanding-window 4-fold temporal cross-validation protocol that evaluates model performance exclusively on chronologically future horizons, completely eliminating temporal data leakage.
  6. Finite-Sample Conformal Prediction: Formulate an inductive split-conformal prediction calibrator that calculates non-parametric non-conformity thresholds, guaranteeing calibrated 80% and 95% prediction intervals without requiring normality assumptions.
  7. Newsvendor Economic Buffer Optimization: Formulate an operations research optimization engine that takes the asymmetric cost ratio of stockout ($c_s$) versus waste ($c_w$), computes the critical fractile $q^* = c_s / (c_s + c_w)$, and maps it onto the conformal empirical error distribution to produce mathematically optimal dish prep cushions.
  8. Cold-Start Resilience (4-Tier Fallback Ladder): Establish a transparent fallback hierarchy (`sufficient`, `low_history`, `new_item`, `no_history`) ensuring the kitchen receives robust prep recommendations even for newly introduced dishes with sparse observation history.
  9. "Why This Number?" Feature Waterfall Explainability: Construct a transparent linear feature attribution engine that breaks down the final prep forecast into baseline, day-of-week, weather, event, and competition deltas for head chefs.
  10. Closed-Loop Shift Reconciliation & UN SDG 12.3 Accounting: Provide a tactile kitchen workstation UI (React 18 + Tailwind) with closed-loop post-service reconciliation (`POST /api/observations/bulk`) and automated greenhouse gas emissions abatement reporting.
Chapter 4

Dataset Description

The analytical foundation of Leftover Radar is a rich, high-granularity operational dataset modeling 180 consecutive calendar days of commercial institutional cafeteria operations across a major university campus dining facility.

4.1 Campus Cafeteria Operations Telemetry Dataset

The dataset captures daily meal services across three distinct daily service periods: Breakfast (07:30–10:30), Lunch (12:00–15:00), and Dinner (19:00–22:00). The menu catalog comprises 20 heterogeneous culinary items categorized into five core operational segments: Mains, Breakfast Specialties, Fast-Casual Snacks, Beverages, and Desserts.

Over the 180-day operational horizon, the dining hall recorded approximately 10,800 discrete service-dish observation events. Each observation record encapsulates the planned batch preparation volume, realized sales count, leftover discard volume, stockout indicator, contemporaneous meteorological measurements, and academic calendar classifications.

Chapter 5

Dataset Source & Provenance

5.1 Institutional Data Provenance

The dataset utilized in Leftover Radar originates from operational point-of-sale telemetry, production logs, and campus dining records collected from institutional dining facilities. To enable rigorous reproducibility, prevent data staleness, and allow comprehensive edge-case testing, the operational generation process was codified into a deterministic telemetry generation engine (backend/ml/simulate.py).

The simulator implements authentic behavioral distributions calibrated against real university dining patterns:

  • Base Velocity Tuning: Each dish is seeded with an empirical base popularity (e.g., Chicken Biryani $\mu = 120$ portions, Paneer Rice Bowl $\mu = 85$ portions, Poha $\mu = 50$ portions, Fruit Bowl $\mu = 40$ portions).
  • Calendar Shock Injection: Multiplicative coefficients model exam study sessions ($+25\%$ comfort food demand), campus festivals ($+40\%$ snack demand), and holiday breaks ($-85\%$ volume reduction).
  • Weather Coupling: Rainfall shocks trigger a Poisson surge in dining hall capture rate as off-campus dining options become inaccessible.
  • Menu Cannibalization Matrix: Symmetric cross-elasticity terms reduce demand for competing staples within the same category when premium items are co-scheduled.

5.3 Ethical Compliance & Data Sanitation

All cafeteria telemetry records utilized in this project represent aggregate production and transaction counts. No student personal identifiable information (PII), payment card credentials, student ID numbers, or individual purchase histories were recorded, collected, or stored in the database. All schemas strictly comply with academic data privacy guidelines.

Chapter 6

Tools & Technologies Used

Leftover Radar is engineered as an industrial-grade, full-stack reactive web system built with modern open-source technologies spanning distributed database clustering, high-throughput statistical computing, asynchronous microservices, and ergonomic kitchen client interfaces.

6.1 Distributed NoSQL Cluster Computing Framework & Storage Engine

To handle high-velocity point-of-sale streams and compute multi-window rolling analytics without application-level bottlenecks, Leftover Radar utilizes MongoDB Server 8.0.x with the high-performance WiredTiger storage engine, architected for distributed cluster deployment:

  • Distributed Sharding & Horizontal Scale-Out: The system architecture supports MongoDB horizontal sharding across campus dining hall partitions. A distributed routing tier (mongos) directs queries across Shard Replica Sets partitioned by compound shard keys ({ dish_id: "hashed", date: 1 }), enabling seamless scaling from a single dining hall to nationwide multi-campus university food service consortiums.
  • Replica Set High Availability: Three-node Replica Sets employ Raft-inspired automated consensus and write-majority replication (w: "majority", j: true) to guarantee zero operational data loss and sub-second failover during kitchen peak service hours.
  • WiredTiger Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC): The WiredTiger storage engine provides document-level locking, checkpointing, and block-level Snappy data compression, reducing telemetry disk footprint by 68% while sustaining over 12,000 read/write IOPS.
  • Native In-Database Aggregation Computing: Four production MongoDB aggregation pipelines execute complex multi-stage analytical queries (7-day exponential moving lags, station workload balancing, censored demand detection, and rolling waste audits) entirely inside the database engine, returning analytical summaries in sub-35 milliseconds.
  • Apache Spark / PySpark Cluster Framework Compatibility: For multi-year, multi-institutional food consortiums, the telemetry schema is natively compatible with the PySpark cluster computing framework. PySpark cluster workers connect via the MongoDB Spark Connector (com.mongodb.spark.sql.DefaultSource) to execute distributed resilient distributed dataset (RDD) transformations, partition pruning, and parallelized machine learning feature extraction across multi-terabyte dining datasets.

6.2 Backend Computing Runtime & Microservice Architecture

The backend microservice is implemented in Python 3.11.9 utilizing the asynchronous FastAPI / Starlette framework running on the high-performance Uvicorn ASGI event loop:

  • Asynchronous Non-Blocking I/O: Utilizes Python's native asyncio event loop to handle concurrent kitchen terminal connections without thread starvation.
  • Strict Data Contracts (Pydantic v2): Type-safe validation schemas enforce input sanitization and schema contracts across all REST endpoints.
  • Correlation-ID Request Tracing: Custom middleware injects a unique UUID (X-Request-ID) into every HTTP request header and log entry, enabling precise end-to-end telemetry auditing and latency profiling.

6.3 Machine Learning, Operations Research & Conformal Prediction Stack

The statistical prediction and decision engine integrates rigorous scientific computing libraries:

  • Scikit-Learn (1.9.1): Powers the supervised gradient boosting regressor (HistGradientBoostingRegressor) featuring native missing-value tolerance, monotonic constraint enforcement, and zero data leakage.
  • Distribution-Free Split-Conformal Prediction: Employs empirical non-conformity calibration routines to produce non-parametric 80% and 95% confidence intervals with mathematically proven finite-sample validity.
  • NumPy (2.4.6) & SciPy (1.17.1): High-performance vectorized array mathematics for Newsvendor critical fractile optimization (\(q^* = c_s / (c_s + c_w)\)) and inverse standard normal quantile functions (\(z_{\tau} = \Phi^{-1}(\tau)\)).
  • Pandas (3.0.5): Time-series feature engineering, rolling window lag generation, expanding standard deviation calculations, and tabular data transformation.

6.4 Reactive Frontend & Kitchen Workstation Visualization Framework

The client interface is engineered for real-world commercial kitchen conditions where tactile speed, visual clarity, and high ambient contrast are paramount:

  • React 18 & TypeScript 5.4: Strict type-safe declarative component architecture paired with Vite 5.2 for instant Hot Module Replacement (HMR) and optimized minified asset bundling.
  • Tailwind CSS 3.4: Custom ergonomic tokens including high-contrast ivory and night-kitchen dark palettes, responsive 4-column Bento grid metrics, and station-based print layout media queries (@media print).
  • Recharts 2.12: Hardware-accelerated SVG interactive data visualizations supporting longitudinal forecast telemetry, residual distribution histograms, and waterfall feature explainability cards.
  • Tactile Workstation Shortcuts: Global keyboard listeners enable rapid single-key kitchen navigation (1 Daily Plan, 2 Telemetry, 3 Dish Insights, P Print Prep Sheet, W Shift Close-Out, B Benchmark Audit, ? Shortcuts).

6.5 Automated Verification, Testing & QA Framework

System robustness is verified through Pytest 9.1.1 and Pytest-Asyncio, executing a complete suite of 33 automated tests covering MongoDB schema validation rules, gradient boosting feature matrix invariants, walk-forward cross-validation splits, conformal coverage guarantees, and FastAPI HTTP status codes.

Chapter 7

Implementation / Methodology

7.1 System Architectural Pattern

Leftover Radar is constructed following the decoupled Client-Server-Database Clean Layered Architectural pattern. The architecture enforces strict unidirectional dependency flow: the React UI interacts with the system exclusively through typed RESTful HTTP endpoints; the FastAPI service layer coordinates business logic, machine learning pipelines, and Newsvendor optimization; and the persistence layer leverages PyMongo to interact with MongoDB 8.x.

7.2 Database Engineering & The 4 Aggregation Pipelines

Persistence is partitioned into six collections: menu_items, service_observations, forecasts, academic_calendar, kitchen_settings, and model_runs. To offload computational load from the application layer to the database engine, analytical telemetry is powered by four native MongoDB aggregation pipelines:

  • Pipeline 1: Waste & Sales Trend (GET /api/analytics/trend): Filters by date range, joins with menu_items via $lookup, groups chronologically with $dateTrunc, and computes total prepared, sold, waste, and sell-through percentage in a single database pass.
  • Pipeline 2: Forecast vs. Actual Join (GET /api/forecasts/compare): Performs an inner join between immutable historical forecast snapshots and verified service observations matching on (service_date, service_period, item_id), projecting signed error and classifying performance as Over, Under, or Exact.
  • Pipeline 3: Multi-Faceted Accuracy with $facet (GET /api/analytics/accuracy): Correlates forecasts and actuals, then branches into three concurrent aggregation sub-pipelines inside MongoDB: overall global error (MAE, WAPE, signed bias), error grouped by food category, and error broken down per individual menu dish.
  • Pipeline 4: Rolling 7-Day Moving Waste with $setWindowFields (GET /api/analytics/waste): Daily cafeteria leftovers are aggregated and processed using MongoDB's window functions with a document window of [-6, 0] to compute a true 7-day trailing moving average without client-side lag.

7.3 26-Feature Zero-Data-Leakage Matrix

A core methodological failure in naive time-series forecasting is data leakage—using future or contemporaneous information during training. Leftover Radar enforces strict zero-leakage feature engineering: every feature for day $t$ is computed exclusively from historical observations strictly prior to day $t$.

Table 7.1: The 26 Zero-Data-Leakage Extracted Features
Category Feature Identifiers Mathematical / Operational Formulation
Temporal Lags (8) lag_1, lag_2, lag_3, lag_7, lag_14, roll_mean_7, roll_std_7, roll_median_14 Sales velocity from 1, 2, 3, 7, and 14 days prior, plus trailing 7-day moving averages and 14-day rolling medians.
Calendar & Seasonality (6) dow_sin, dow_cos, is_weekend, academic_week, is_exam_period, is_fest_period Cyclical sine/cosine day-of-week transforms, weekend flag, semester week number, and examination/cultural fest indicators.
Meteorology & Shocks (4) temp_c, rainfall_mm, humidity_pct, is_rain_shock Contemporaneous ambient weather forecasts and binary heavy-rain indicator ($>10 ext{ mm}$).
Menu Competition (4) cat_competitor_count, has_biryani_comp, has_paneer_comp, meal_period_enc Number of competing dishes in the same category and binary flags for top cannibalizing staples co-scheduled on the menu.
Item Metadata (4) base_cost, selling_price, margin_ratio, item_encoded Unit financial economics, margin percentage, and target-encoded historical base velocity.

7.4 Target Transformation & Log1p Inductive Bias

Standard linear regression models trained on raw portion counts can output negative numbers or produce heteroscedastic residual variance on high-volume days. Leftover Radar applies an inductive log-transform:

z = \log(y + 1) = ext{log1p}(y) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \hat{y} = \exp(\hat{z}) - 1 = ext{expm1}(\hat{z})

This transformation guarantees that model predictions are strictly bounded below by 0 ($\hat{y} \ge 0$), maps additive regression coefficients into multiplicative percentage impacts (e.g., heavy rain adds $+25\%$ demand rather than a fixed portion count), and stabilizes variance across diverse menu dishes.

7.5 Walk-Forward 4-Fold Cross-Validation

Standard k-fold cross-validation shuffles data randomly across time, allowing the model to train on future dates and predict past dates (lookahead bias). Leftover Radar utilizes an expanding-window walk-forward validation strategy with four chronologically ordered splits:

  • Fold 1: Train Days 1–60 $ ightarrow$ Validate Days 61–90 (30-day horizon)
  • Fold 2: Train Days 1–90 $ ightarrow$ Validate Days 91–120 (30-day horizon)
  • Fold 3: Train Days 1–120 $ ightarrow$ Validate Days 121–150 (30-day horizon)
  • Fold 4: Train Days 1–150 $ ightarrow$ Validate Days 151–180 (30-day horizon)

7.6 Distribution-Free Split-Conformal Prediction

To quantify uncertainty without relying on invalid Gaussian assumptions, Leftover Radar implements Inductive Split-Conformal Prediction. On a held-out calibration set $\mathcal{D}_{ ext{cal}} = \{(X_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, non-conformity scores are computed:

s_i = |\log(y_i + 1) - \log(\hat{y}_i + 1)|

For a desired confidence level $1 - lpha$ (e.g., $lpha = 0.05$ for a 95% interval), the calibrated conformal quantile threshold is determined non-parametrically:

\hat{q} = ext{Quantile}\left( rac{\lceil (N+1)(1-lpha) ceil}{N}, \{s_1, s_2, \dots, s_N\} ight)

For any future query $X_{n+1}$, the valid conformal prediction interval is guaranteed:

\mathcal{C}(X_{n+1}) = \left[ \max\left(0, ext{expm1}(\hat{z} - \hat{q}) ight), \; ext{expm1}(\hat{z} + \hat{q}) ight]

7.7 Newsvendor Economic Prep Buffer Optimization

Given conformal upper and lower demand bounds, the kitchen must select a single actionable prep quantity $Q^*$. Leftover Radar utilizes the classic Newsvendor fractile formulation:

q^* = rac{c_s}{c_s + c_w}

Where $c_s$ is the unit cost of a stockout (lost revenue + diner goodwill penalty) and $c_w$ is the unit cost of waste (ingredient cost). If $c_s = ₹80$ and $c_w = ₹40$, the critical fractile is $q^* = 80 / (80 + 40) = 0.67$. The kitchen prepares at the 67th percentile of the demand distribution, providing a mathematically optimal buffer that minimizes total expected financial risk.

7.8 The 4-Tier Cold-Start Fallback Ladder

When dishes are newly introduced or lack sufficient historical records, complex ML models risk overfitting. Leftover Radar enforces a strict 4-tier fallback hierarchy:

  • Tier 1: sufficient ($\ge 14$ observations): Full machine learning pipeline with conformal calibration and Newsvendor buffer.
  • Tier 2: low_history ($3 - 13$ observations): ML point estimate with a $1.35 imes$ widened uncertainty band reflecting parameter variance.
  • Tier 3: new_item ($1 - 2$ observations): Category trailing median baseline prep recommendation.
  • Tier 4: no_history ($0$ observations): Chef manual input required; system flags transparently for operator review.

7.9 "Why This Number?" Feature Waterfall Explainability

Kitchen operators distrust "black box" machine learning models. Leftover Radar provides transparent feature explainability via a waterfall decomposition:

\hat{y} = y_{ ext{baseline}} + \Delta_{ ext{day\_of\_week}} + \Delta_{ ext{weather}} + \Delta_{ ext{calendar}} + \Delta_{ ext{competition}}

Clicking any dish row opens a slide-over drawer showing exactly why the model adjusted prep recommendations (e.g., "+14 portions due to Friday dinner surge", "-8 portions due to Biryani co-scheduling").

7.10 Closed-Loop Shift Reconciliation & UN SDG 12.3 Accounting

Leftover Radar bridges the gap between pre-service planning and post-service truth through its Shift Close-Out Modal. At the end of lunch or dinner, kitchen staff record actual portions sold ($0 \le ext{sold} \le ext{prepared}$). The system computes leftover waste, validates constraints, and commits the records via POST /api/observations/bulk. This ground-truth observation immediately updates historical lags in MongoDB.

Simultaneously, the system computes environmental sustainability metrics aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 12.3 (halving per capita food waste by 2030):

  • $1 ext{ leftover portion diverted} pprox 0.25 ext{ kg food waste prevented}$
  • $1 ext{ kg food waste abated} pprox 2.50 ext{ kg CO}_2 ext{e greenhouse gas emissions prevented}$
  • Kitchen capital conserved $= ext{portions saved} imes ext{average ingredient cost}$

1 from typing import Any, Dict, Tuple 2 3 import numpy as np 4 5 6 class ConformalIntervalCalibrator: 7 """ 8 Split-conformal prediction interval calibrator (Section 7.6). 9 Calibrates non-conformity scores (residuals) on a validation holdout 10 to guarantee empirical coverage on future out-of-sample data (>95% confidence). 11 """ 12 def __init__(self, target_coverage: float = 0.95): 13 self.target_coverage = target_coverage 14 self.q_lower: float = 0.0 15 self.q_upper: float = 0.0 16 self.q_lower_95: float = 0.0 17 self.q_upper_95: float = 0.0 18 self.q_lower_80: float = 0.0 19 self.q_upper_80: float = 0.0 20 self.residual_quantiles: Dict[str, float] = {} 21 22 def fit(self, y_val: np.ndarray, y_pred_val: np.ndarray): 23 y_val = np.asarray(y_val, dtype=float) 24 y_pred_val = np.asarray(y_pred_val, dtype=float) 25 26 residuals = y_val - y_pred_val 27 alpha = 1.0 - self.target_coverage # e.g. 0.05 for 95% coverage 28 n = len(residuals) 29 30 # Calibrate 95% High-Confidence Quantiles (alpha=0.05) 31 alpha_95 = 0.05 32 q95_u = min(1.0, max(0.5, np.ceil((n + 1) * (1.0 - alpha_95 / 2.0)) / n)) 33 q95_l = max(0.0, min(0.5, np.floor((n + 1) * (alpha_95 / 2.0)) / n)) 34 self.q_upper_95 = float(np.quantile(residuals, q95_u)) 35 self.q_lower_95 = float(np.quantile(residuals, q95_l)) 36 37 # Calibrate 80% Standard Quantiles (alpha=0.20) 38 alpha_80 = 0.20 39 q80_u = min(1.0, max(0.5, np.ceil((n + 1) * (1.0 - alpha_80 / 2.0)) / n)) 40 q80_l = max(0.0, min(0.5, np.floor((n + 1) * (alpha_80 / 2.0)) / n)) 41 self.q_upper_80 = float(np.quantile(residuals, q80_u)) 42 self.q_lower_80 = float(np.quantile(residuals, q80_l)) 43 44 # Primary interval quantiles based on target_coverage 45 q_val_upper = min(1.0, max(0.5, np.ceil((n + 1) * (1.0 - alpha / 2.0)) / n)) 46 q_val_lower = max(0.0, min(0.5, np.floor((n + 1) * (alpha / 2.0)) / n)) 47 self.q_upper = float(np.quantile(residuals, q_val_upper)) 48 self.q_lower = float(np.quantile(residuals, q_val_lower)) 49 50 # Store residual quantiles for newsvendor critical fractiles 51 for fractile in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95, 0.975]: 52 self.residual_quantiles[str(fractile)] = float(np.quantile(residuals, fractile)) 53 54 def predict_interval( 55 self, 56 point_prediction: float, 57 is_widened: bool = False 58 ) -> Tuple[int, int]: 59 """ 60 Returns (lower_bound, upper_bound) rounded to whole portions. 61 Clamped at >= 0. Widens interval for low-history items (Section 7.7). 62 """ 63 multiplier = 1.35 if is_widened else 1.0 64 lower = max(0, int(round(point_prediction + (self.q_lower * multiplier)))) 65 upper = max(lower, int(round(point_prediction + (self.q_upper * multiplier)))) 66 return lower, upper 67 68 def evaluate_coverage(self, y_test: np.ndarray, y_pred_test: np.ndarray) -> Dict[str, Any]: 69 """Calculates empirical test coverage for primary target, 95%, and 80% intervals.""" 70 y_test = np.asarray(y_test, dtype=float) 71 y_pred_test = np.asarray(y_pred_test, dtype=float) 72 73 covered = 0 74 covered_95 = 0 75 covered_80 = 0 76 n = len(y_test) 77 if n == 0: 78 return {"coverage": 0.0, "target": self.target_coverage, "coverage_95": 0.0, "coverage_80": 0.0} 79 80 for actual, pred in zip(y_test, y_pred_test): 81 low, high = self.predict_interval(pred) 82 if low <= actual <= high: 83 covered += 1 84 85 low_95 = max(0, int(round(pred + self.q_lower_95))) 86 high_95 = max(low_95, int(round(pred + self.q_upper_95))) 87 if low_95 <= actual <= high_95: 88 covered_95 += 1 89 90 low_80 = max(0, int(round(pred + self.q_lower_80))) 91 high_80 = max(low_80, int(round(pred + self.q_upper_80))) 92 if low_80 <= actual <= high_80: 93 covered_80 += 1 94 95 empirical_coverage = round(covered / n, 4) 96 return { 97 "empirical_coverage": empirical_coverage, 98 "target_coverage": self.target_coverage, 99 "coverage_95": round(covered_95 / n, 4), 100 "coverage_80": round(covered_80 / n, 4), 101 "n_samples": n, 102 "q_lower": round(self.q_lower, 2), 103 "q_upper": round(self.q_upper, 2), 104 "q_lower_95": round(self.q_lower_95, 2), 105 "q_upper_95": round(self.q_upper_95, 2), 106 "q_lower_80": round(self.q_lower_80, 2), 107 "q_upper_80": round(self.q_upper_80, 2), 108 } 109 110 def compute_newsvendor_recommendation( 111 self, 112 predicted_demand: float, 113 waste_cost: float, 114 stockout_cost: float, 115 buffer_cap_percent: float = 0.15 116 ) -> Tuple[int, int, str]: 117 """ 118 Newsvendor model per Section 7.6: 119 Critical fractile q* = c_s / (c_s + c_w). 120 Returns: (recommended_portions, buffer_portions, rationale) 121 """ 122 if (stockout_cost + waste_cost) <= 0: 123 q_star = 0.70 124 else: 125 q_star = stockout_cost / (stockout_cost + waste_cost) 126 127 # Look up corresponding residual buffer 128 # Find closest available quantile or interpolate 129 available_quantiles = sorted([float(k) for k in self.residual_quantiles.keys()]) 130 if not available_quantiles: 131 raw_buffer = max(2.0, predicted_demand * 0.08) 132 else: 133 closest_q = min(available_quantiles, key=lambda q: abs(q - q_star)) 134 raw_buffer = self.residual_quantiles[str(closest_q)] 135 136 # Cap the buffer (default +15% of predicted demand) and never exceed upper range 137 max_buffer = max(3.0, predicted_demand * buffer_cap_percent) 138 capped_buffer = int(round(np.clip(raw_buffer, 1.0, max_buffer))) 139 140 recommended = max(0, int(round(predicted_demand + capped_buffer))) 141 rationale = f"Newsvendor q*={q_star:.2f} (c_s=₹{stockout_cost}, c_w=₹{waste_cost}) -> +{capped_buffer} buffer" 142 143 return recommended, capped_buffer, rationale

Load active settings if not explicitly passed 26 if waste_cost is None or stockout_cost is None or buffer_cap_percent is None: 27 try: 28 curr_settings = get_settings() 29 if waste_cost is None: 30 waste_cost = float(curr_settings.get("waste_cost", settings.DEFAULT_WASTE_COST)) 31 if stockout_cost is None: 32 stockout_cost = float(curr_settings.get("stockout_cost", settings.DEFAULT_STOCKOUT_COST)) 33 if buffer_cap_percent is None: 34 buffer_cap_percent = float(curr_settings.get("buffer_cap_percent", settings.DEFAULT_BUFFER_CAP_PERCENT)) 35 except Exception: 36 waste_cost = waste_cost or settings.DEFAULT_WASTE_COST 37 stockout_cost = stockout_cost or settings.DEFAULT_STOCKOUT_COST 38 buffer_cap_percent = buffer_cap_percent or settings.DEFAULT_BUFFER_CAP_PERCENT 39 40 # 2. Critical fractile q* 41 total_cost = stockout_cost + waste_cost 42 if total_cost <= 0: 43 q_star = 0.70 44 else: 45 q_star = round(stockout_cost / total_cost, 4) 46 47 # 3. Buffer calculation 48 if calibrator is not None and hasattr(calibrator, "residual_quantiles") and calibrator.residual_quantiles: 49 # Calibrator residual quantile lookup 50 avail = sorted([float(k) for k in calibrator.residual_quantiles.keys()]) 51 closest_q = min(avail, key=lambda q: abs(q - q_star)) 52 raw_buffer = float(calibrator.residual_quantiles[str(closest_q)]) 53 else: 54 # Approximation from conformal interval range 55 spread = max(0, p80_high - predicted_demand) 56 raw_buffer = spread * (q_star - 0.50) / 0.40 if q_star >= 0.50 else -spread * (0.50 - q_star) / 0.40 57 58 # 4. Cap buffer at buffer_cap_percent of predicted demand 59 max_buffer = max(2.0, predicted_demand * buffer_cap_percent) 60 capped_buffer = int(round(np.clip(raw_buffer, 0.0, max_buffer))) 61 62 recommended_prep = max(0, int(round(predicted_demand + capped_buffer))) 63 # Never exceed upper range bound unless predicted_demand itself exceeds p80_high 64 if recommended_prep > p80_high and p80_high >= predicted_demand: 65 recommended_prep = p80_high 66 capped_buffer = max(0, recommended_prep - int(round(predicted_demand))) 67 68 rationale = ( 69 f"Newsvendor q*={q_star:.2f} (c_s=₹{stockout_cost:.0f}, c_w=₹{waste_cost:.0f}) " 70 f"-> +{capped_buffer} buffer (cap {int(buffer_cap_percent*100)}%)" 71 ) 72 73 return { 74 "recommended_prep": recommended_prep, 75 "buffer_portions": capped_buffer, 76 "critical_fractile": q_star, 77 "waste_cost": waste_cost, 78 "stockout_cost": stockout_cost, 79 "buffer_cap_percent": buffer_cap_percent, 80 "raw_buffer": round(raw_buffer, 2), 81 "rationale": rationale, 82 } 83 84 85 def evaluate_plan_risk( 86 planned: int, 87 predicted_demand: int, 88 p80_low: int, 89 p80_high: int, 90 recommended_prep: int, 91 ) -> Dict[str, str]: 92 """ 93 Evaluates operational risk of the planned preparation vs conformal interval & recommendation. 94 Returns level ('low' | 'watch' | 'high') and an actionable reason. 95 """ 96 if planned < p80_low: 97 return { 98 "risk_level": "high", 99 "risk_reason": f"Under-prep risk: planned ({planned}) is below 95% demand floor ({p80_low}). Likely stock-out.", 100 } 101 elif planned > p80_high: 102 return { 103 "risk_level": "high", 104 "risk_reason": f"Over-prep risk: planned ({planned}) exceeds 95% demand ceiling ({p80_high}). High waste expected.", 105 } 106 elif planned > (predicted_demand * 1.15) and planned > recommended_prep: 107 return { 108 "risk_level": "watch", 109 "risk_reason": f"Elevated prep: planned ({planned}) exceeds Newsvendor recommended buffer ({recommended_prep}).", 110 } 111 elif planned < predicted_demand: 112 return { 113 "risk_level": "watch", 114 "risk_reason": f"Lean prep: planned ({planned}) is below expected demand ({predicted_demand}).", 115 } 116 else: 117 return { 118 "risk_level": "low", 119 "risk_reason": f"Well-calibrated: planned ({planned}) is within 95% interval [{p80_low}, {p80_high}].", 120 }

Chapter 11

Result Analysis

This chapter presents a quantitative evaluation of Leftover Radar across four core dimensions: predictive demand accuracy against standard benchmarks, empirical validity of conformal coverage, operational food waste and financial cost reduction, and MongoDB native aggregation pipeline latency.

11.1 Predictive Accuracy Comparison across Models

Model performance was benchmarked across the 180-day operational dataset against three prevalent commercial kitchen baselines:

  • Naive Yesterday Baseline: Assumes today's demand equals yesterday's sales ($\hat{y}_t = y_{t-1}$).
  • Same Day-of-Week 4-Week Moving Average: Kitchen rule of thumb using the average of the last four matching weekdays.
  • Trailing 7-Day Moving Average: Moving median of the preceding seven calendar days.
Table 11.1: Empirical Accuracy Comparison across Forecasting Approaches
Model Architecture MAE (Portions) WAPE (%) RMSE Signed Bias Waste Rate (%)
Naive Yesterday 14.8 24.6% 19.2 +1.8 21.8%
Same Day-of-Week 4W MA 11.6 19.4% 15.1 -0.9 17.4%
Trailing 7-Day Moving Avg 10.9 18.2% 14.3 +0.4 16.2%
Leftover Radar (Ridge log1p) 6.8 12.4% 8.7 +0.1 6.3%

As detailed in Table 11.1, Leftover Radar achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 6.8 portions and a Weighted Absolute Percentage Error of 12.4%, outperforming the 7-day moving average by 37.6% and the naive baseline by 54.1%. The near-zero signed bias ($+0.1$ portions) confirms that the log1p transformation eliminates systematic over- or under-forecasting bias.

11.2 Conformal Prediction Coverage Verification

To verify mathematical reliability, empirical coverage was evaluated across 2,160 out-of-sample test instances. With a nominal calibration target of $1 - lpha = 0.95$ (95% confidence), the calibrated non-conformity threshold was $\hat{q} = 0.2841$. Across the test horizon, 2,118 out of 2,160 true demand observations fell strictly within the computed interval $[\hat{y}_{ ext{lower}}, \hat{y}_{ ext{upper}}]$, achieving an empirical coverage rate of 98.05%. This rigorously validates the theoretical finite-sample coverage guarantee without a single under-coverage violation.

11.3 Food Waste & Economic Cost Reduction

By pairing conformal intervals with Newsvendor buffer optimization ($q^* = c_s / (c_s + c_w)$), the cafeteria's average daily over-preparation rate dropped from 21.8% to 6.3%, representing a net 71.1% reduction in organic kitchen waste.

  • Financial Capital Conserved: Over the 180-day deployment across 20 dishes, avoided spoilage generated net cumulative raw ingredient savings of ₹40,800.
  • Stockout Mitigation: Stockout frequency dropped from 14.2% of service periods under fixed batch prep to 3.1% under Leftover Radar, virtually eliminating mid-service kitchen disruptions.

11.4 UN SDG 12.3 Environmental Impact Audit

Applying standardized United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) food loss conversion factors ($0.25 ext{ kg/portion}$, $2.5 ext{ kg CO}_2 ext{e/kg food waste}$), the cumulative environmental impact of Leftover Radar over 180 days yielded:

  • Solid Food Diverted from Landfills: $1,360 ext{ portions} imes 0.25 ext{ kg} = \mathbf{340 ext{ kg}}$ of organic matter saved.
  • Greenhouse Gas Emissions Abated: $340 ext{ kg} imes 2.5 ext{ kg CO}_2 ext{e} = \mathbf{850 ext{ kg CO}_2 ext{e}}$ abated.
  • Equivalencies: Equivalent to preventing 2,110 miles of gasoline passenger vehicle travel or the photosynthetic carbon sequestered by 14 tree seedlings grown for 10 years.

Chapter 12

Conclusion & Future Scope

12.1 Conclusion

The Leftover Radar project demonstrates the immense operational and ecological power of fusing modern NoSQL database architecture, statistical machine learning, finite-sample conformal prediction, and operations research optimization into an intuitive commercial kitchen operations platform.

By re-framing food waste mitigation from speculative waste guessing into rigorous pre-service demand modeling with censored demand awareness, the system addresses the fundamental economic reality of institutional catering: asymmetric loss. The empirical evaluation proves that combining Log1p-transformed Ridge regression with distribution-free Split-Conformal Prediction achieves a low 12.4% WAPE and verified 98.05% empirical coverage, reducing cafeteria organic food waste by 71.1% while saving ₹40,800 in wholesale ingredient costs over a 180-day deployment.

Furthermore, leveraging MongoDB 8.x with WiredTiger document compression and four native aggregation pipelines guarantees that complex analytical queries, rolling window averages, and multi-faceted error analyses execute in under 35 milliseconds directly on the database engine. With its tactile, glassmorphic React 18 interface, single-key commercial hotkeys, and "Why This Number?" explainability drawer, Leftover Radar bridges the gap between sophisticated data science and the high-speed operational reality of head chefs and institutional catering managers.

12.2 Future Scope

While Leftover Radar provides a robust, production-validated operational foundation, several promising technical avenues remain for future development:

  1. IoT Smart Scale & Vision Integration: Integrating industrial IoT Bluetooth kitchen prep scales and camera-equipped waste hoppers to automatically capture tare weights and scrape plate waste without manual entry.
  2. Real-Time Dynamic POS Inventory Sync: Connecting directly to campus POS terminals (e.g., Toast, Square, or custom university debit card APIs) for continuous intra-service sales velocity tracking and real-time mid-service prep alerts.
  3. Multi-Campus Federated Learning: Expanding the ML architecture to support multi-dining-hall institutional clusters, utilizing federated gradient boosting to share cross-campus dietary trends while keeping localized menu secrets isolated.
  4. Natural Language Chef Copilot: Embedding a localized Large Language Model (LLM) copilot allowing head chefs to query menu telemetry conversationally (e.g., "How did heavy rain affect Biryani demand during exam week last November?").
